div.head: I Atr 1.13
div.ab: Gif him seo lad byrste, gylde þam cynge his were, ⁊ sy se man útlah.
Gyf him seo lad byrste, gylde ðam cynge his were, ⁊ si se man utlah.
Si lada frangat ei, reddat regi weram suam, et sit homo forsbannitus apud omnes (homines).
Gyf him seo lad byrste, gylde ðam cynge his were ⁊ si se man utlah.
Wenn ihm diese Reinigung misslingt, zahle er dem König sein Wergeld. Und jener [Untergebene] sei friedlos.
If this clearing fails him, let him pay the king his wergild. And let that [dependant] be an outlaw.
If he fail to clear himself, he shall pay his (own) wergeld to the king, and the man shall be an outlaw.

note.seg: Im Ggs. zu 1, 9a ist hier das Wergeld des Herrn gemeint, eine härtere Strafe, weil dieser nicht bloss wie dort Gefolgsherr war, sondern polizeilich verantwortlich für die Hausinsassen. Wäre nur des Diebes Wergeld gemeint, so litte ja der Begünstiger nicht mehr Schaden als nach 1, 11 der an der Flucht Unbeteiligte. Deutlich scheidend bestimmt Hn 41, 6 weram illius bei Unachtsamkeit, weram suam beim Verhelfen zur Flucht; vgl. 12, 3; Gl Begünstigung 2. 15a mit der Korrektur o. zu 1, 9a². Richtig also versteht Q hier und zu II Cn 31, 2 (= Hn 41, 6. Leis Wl 52) sowie dort Inst Cn des Herrn Wergeld; nur Cons Cn missversteht dort das des Flüchtlings

In contrast to 1, 9a, the lord’s wergild is meant here, a harsher penalty, because he was not merely, as there, the lord of a follower, but was responsible in matters of police for the members of his household. If only the thief’s wergild were meant, the harbourer would suffer no more loss than, under 1, 11, the man who had no part in the flight. Hn 41, 6 clearly distinguishes weram illius for negligence from weram suam for aiding the escape; cf. 12, 3; Gl Begünstigung 2. 15a with the correction above on 1, 9a². Q therefore rightly understands the lord’s wergild here and at II Cn 31, 2 (= Hn 41, 6. Leis Wl 52), as does Inst Cn there; only Cons Cn there misunderstands it as that of the fugitive

Liebermann points out that the wergeld here is the lord’s own because, as distinct from the case treated in § 11, the lord in this instance has been an accessory to the man’s flight. He refers to Hn. 41, 6–11 where the distinction is clearly expressed, e.g. in 41, 8: Si accusetur et aufugiat, reddat dominus eius regi weram illius hominis, and 41, 10: Si iuramentum frangat ei, reddat weram suam regi; et qui fugit utlaga sit.
